title: Diseases of Endocrine Hyperfunction
subject: Endocrine System (ENDO)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers diseases in which a gland makes too much hormone: Cushing syndrome, primary and secondary hyperaldosteronism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, primary, secondary, and tertiary hyperparathyroidism, familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, gigantism and acromegaly, Graves disease and toxic multinodular goiter, SIADH, and precocious puberty. Every one of them is solved the same way. First ask whether the hormone is escaping its normal feedback, then read the paired trophic or regulatory signal (ACTH, renin, PTH with calcium, TSH, LH and FSH) to find the source, and finally explain each sign from what the hormone normally does. Board questions give a lab panel and ask for the lesion, or give a lesion and ask for the panel.

sections.title: Finding the source of Cushing syndrome

blocks.text: Cushing syndrome is the clinical state of chronic glucocorticoid excess from any cause. The most common cause overall is exogenous glucocorticoid therapy. Among endogenous causes, an ACTH-secreting pituitary corticotroph adenoma, usually a microadenoma under 10 mm, accounts for about 70% and is called Cushing disease. Ectopic ACTH, most often from small cell lung carcinoma or a bronchial carcinoid, and primary adrenal adenoma or carcinoma make up most of the rest.

Once cortisol excess is proven (C02), the question is whether ACTH is driving it. Plasma ACTH answers this. When the adrenal is the source, or the patient takes glucocorticoids, cortisol suppresses the hypothalamus and corticotrophs, so ACTH is low. When a pituitary adenoma or ectopic tumor is the source, ACTH is normal or high, and its trophic effect produces bilateral adrenal cortical hyperplasia. The adrenal morphology follows directly: a cortisol-secreting adenoma leaves the opposite gland and the adjacent cortex atrophic, and exogenous steroids leave both glands atrophic.

High-dose dexamethasone then separates pituitary from ectopic ACTH. A corticotroph adenoma is not fully autonomous; its feedback set point is raised, so a large dose of glucocorticoid (8 mg) still lowers ACTH and cortisol, classically by more than 50%. Ectopic tumors and adrenal tumors do not respond. Some well-differentiated carcinoids do suppress, so imaging and, where needed, inferior petrosal sinus sampling (a central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient means a pituitary source) settle doubtful cases.

Very high ACTH levels also explain two clues to an ectopic source. ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone both come from proopiomelanocortin and both activate the melanocortin 1 receptor on melanocytes, causing hyperpigmentation. Very high cortisol saturates renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, so cortisol activates mineralocorticoid receptors and causes marked hypokalemia. Ectopic disease often develops too fast for the classic body habitus to form. Adrenal carcinoma, unlike adenoma, often secretes androgens as well and causes virilization.

blocks.predict: A smoker loses weight over three months, develops severe hypokalemia and hyperpigmentation, but has no striae or central obesity. Plasma cortisol is very high. Is this Cushing syndrome, and where is the ACTH coming from?
blocks.explain: Yes. The very high ACTH from an ectopic source, likely small cell lung carcinoma, causes pigmentation through the melanocortin 1 receptor, and the huge cortisol load overwhelms 11-beta-HSD2 and acts as a mineralocorticoid. The course is too rapid and catabolic for fat redistribution and striae to develop. High-dose dexamethasone would not suppress cortisol.

sections.title: Manifestations of cortisol excess and screening tests

blocks.text: Cortisol is a catabolic, gluconeogenic hormone that acts through the intracellular glucocorticoid receptor, a ligand-activated transcription factor. Its normal job in stress is to supply glucose: it breaks down muscle protein to provide amino acids, induces hepatic gluconeogenic enzymes such as phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, and reduces insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in muscle and fat. Sustained excess turns these adaptive actions into disease.

Fat redistribution is the most visible change. Cortisol promotes lipolysis in the limbs, while the combination of cortisol and the hyperinsulinemia caused by insulin resistance favors fat storage in visceral, facial, dorsocervical, and supraclavicular depots, which have more glucocorticoid receptors and 11-beta-HSD1 activity. The result is central obesity with thin limbs, moon facies, and a dorsocervical fat pad.

Loss of protein and inhibition of fibroblasts explain the skin, muscle, and bone. The dermis thins because collagen synthesis falls, so expanding fat stretches it into wide (often over 1 cm) purple striae, colored by the venous blood visible through thin skin, and minor trauma causes bruising. Proximal muscles waste and weaken, with selective atrophy of type II (fast) fibers. Bone loss follows from suppressed osteoblast function, reduced intestinal calcium absorption, and increased urinary calcium loss. Wound healing is slow because fibroblast activity and inflammation are suppressed, and infections are more frequent.

blocks.text: Screening: proving loss of normal regulation

A single random cortisol is useless because secretion is pulsatile and has a strong circadian rhythm, peaking in the early morning and falling to a nadir near midnight. Screening tests therefore look for the features of autonomy. The 24-hour urine free cortisol measures unbound cortisol filtered over a whole day, an integrated measure of excess. Late-night salivary cortisol detects loss of the midnight trough, an early abnormality. The overnight low-dose (1 mg) dexamethasone suppression test checks feedback: in a normal person morning cortisol falls below about 1.8 micrograms/dL (50 nmol/L), whereas any form of Cushing syndrome fails to suppress. Two concordant abnormal tests are usually required, because depression, alcohol use, severe obesity, and acute illness can produce mild false positives (pseudo-Cushing states).

Aldosterone is made in the zona glomerulosa in response to angiotensin II and plasma K+. It binds the mineralocorticoid receptor in principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct and increases apical ENaC channels, basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, and apical ROMK K+ channels. Na+ entering through ENaC leaves the lumen electrically negative, which drives K+ secretion through ROMK. Aldosterone also stimulates the H+-ATPase of alpha-intercalated cells.

In primary hyperaldosteronism the adrenal makes aldosterone without regard to renin. Bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia is now the more common cause, and an aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn syndrome) most of the rest. Sodium retention expands volume and raises blood pressure, and the expanded volume suppresses renin. The classic triad is hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis with high aldosterone and low renin, so a high aldosterone to renin ratio is the screening clue. Many patients are normokalemic at diagnosis, so a normal K+ does not exclude it.

blocks.title: From autonomous aldosterone to the lab picture
steps: Adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia secretes aldosterone independently

blocks.caption: Hypokalemia itself sustains the alkalosis by shifting H+ into cells and increasing renal ammoniagenesis.

blocks.text: Edema is absent because of aldosterone escape. After a few days of sodium retention, the higher arterial pressure causes pressure natriuresis and stretched atria release natriuretic peptides, so sodium excretion returns to match intake at a slightly larger volume. Potassium and hydrogen ion wasting continue because distal Na+ delivery stays high. Hypokalemia causes muscle weakness, polyuria from reduced collecting duct response to ADH, and U waves on the ECG.

In secondary hyperaldosteronism the stimulus is renin. Renal hypoperfusion or low effective arterial volume activates the renin-angiotensin system, so renin and aldosterone are both high. Renal artery stenosis and renin-secreting tumors cause it with hypertension; heart failure, cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome cause it with edema; and diuretics or vomiting cause it with low or normal pressure.

blocks.title: Reading renin and aldosterone together
rows: Renal artery stenosis, heart failure, cirrhosis, diuretics
Cushing syndrome, 11-beta- and 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency, licorice, Liddle syndrome
blocks.caption: Hypertension with hypokalemia always prompts this three-way split.

blocks.predict: Two hypertensive patients have hypokalemia and high aldosterone. One has an abdominal bruit and high renin; the other has low renin. Which has an adrenal lesion?
blocks.explain: The low-renin patient. Autonomous aldosterone expands volume and suppresses renin. In the patient with a bruit, renal artery stenosis lowers pressure at the juxtaglomerular apparatus, so renin rises first and drives aldosterone, a secondary form.

blocks.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is a group of autosomal recessive defects in enzymes needed to make cortisol. Low cortisol removes negative feedback, ACTH rises, and chronic ACTH stimulation enlarges both adrenal cortices. Steroid precursors pile up behind the block and are pushed into any pathway that remains open. Every finding can be predicted from two questions: which products are missing, and which products are being overmade.

blocks.title: General logic of congenital adrenal hyperplasia
steps: Enzyme defect blocks cortisol synthesis
Low cortisol removes feedback; ACTH rises
ACTH causes bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
Precursors accumulate behind the block
Precursors shunted into open pathways
Deficient and excess products set the phenotype
blocks.caption: ACTH can also drive skin pigmentation, most obvious in the 21-hydroxylase form.

blocks.text: 21-hydroxylase (CYP21A2) deficiency causes over 90% of cases. The enzyme converts progesterone to 11-deoxycorticosterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone to 11-deoxycortisol, so both the mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid arms are blocked. 17-hydroxyprogesterone, the diagnostic marker, accumulates and is diverted through 17,20-lyase to adrenal androgens. In the classic salt-wasting form, aldosterone deficiency causes Na+ loss, hypovolemia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and high renin, usually presenting as a crisis in the first weeks of life. Girls (46,XX) are born with ambiguous, virilized external genitalia but normal internal female organs; boys look normal at birth and may present with salt wasting or later with early virilization. Milder forms present as simple virilizing or nonclassic disease with hirsutism and irregular menses.

11-beta-hydroxylase (CYP11B1) deficiency blocks the final step to cortisol. 11-deoxycortisol and 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC) accumulate, and androgens rise. DOC is a potent mineralocorticoid, so instead of salt wasting the patient has hypertension and hypokalemia with low renin and low aldosterone, together with virilization.

17-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP17A1) deficiency blocks entry into both the cortisol and the sex steroid pathways. Pregnenolone is diverted to DOC and corticosterone, producing hypertension and hypokalemia with low renin and aldosterone. Corticosterone has enough glucocorticoid activity to prevent adrenal crisis. Without sex steroids, 46,XY individuals are undervirilized with female-appearing external genitalia, and 46,XX individuals have no puberty and primary amenorrhea.

blocks.title: The three CAH forms
blocks.caption: Androgens decide genital findings; DOC versus aldosterone deficiency decides blood pressure and K+.

blocks.title: Predicting a CAH variant
blocks.text: A 15-year-old with female external genitalia, no breast development, and blood pressure 160/100 mm Hg has K+ 2.9 mEq/L and low renin. Hypertension with low K+ and low renin means a mineralocorticoid other than aldosterone is in excess, which points to 11-beta- or 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency. Virilization would mean 11-beta. Absent puberty means no sex steroids, so the block is at 17-alpha-hydroxylase. Karyotype may be 46,XX or 46,XY; in either case no estrogen is made, and a 46,XY patient was undervirilized in utero because no testosterone was made. DOC is high, cortisol is low, and corticosterone prevents crisis.

PTH raises plasma ionized calcium in three ways. It stimulates osteoblasts to express RANKL, which activates osteoclasts and releases calcium and phosphate from bone. It increases calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule and reduces phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule by removing NaPi-IIa cotransporters. It also stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, and the resulting calcitriol increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption. Normally a rise in calcium acts on the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) of chief cells to suppress PTH.

In primary hyperparathyroidism the gland escapes this feedback. A single parathyroid adenoma causes about 85% of cases, multigland hyperplasia about 10% (including MEN1 and MEN2A), and carcinoma about 1%. The laboratory signature is hypercalcemia with a PTH that is high or inappropriately normal, since any detectable PTH is abnormal when calcium is high. Phosphate is low or low-normal because of PTH phosphaturia. PTH also reduces proximal bicarbonate reabsorption, so a mild hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis may occur, and alkaline phosphatase rises when bone turnover is high. In hypercalcemia of malignancy, by contrast, PTH is suppressed.

Calcium on CaSR in the thick ascending limb reduces NaCl reabsorption and the collecting duct responds less to ADH
Bone pain, fractures, raised alkaline phosphatase
Sustained osteoclastic resorption, mainly of cortical bone

blocks.caption: The older summary is stones, bones, abdominal groans, and psychiatric overtones; most cases today are found on routine chemistry while asymptomatic.

blocks.text: Hypercalcemia raises the threshold for opening voltage-gated Na+ channels by screening negative surface charges on the membrane, so nerves and muscle become less excitable. This single mechanism explains the weakness, constipation, and mental slowing.
Osteitis fibrosa cystica

Severe or long-standing disease produces osteitis fibrosa cystica. Osteoclasts tunnel into trabeculae and resorb cortical bone, the marrow is replaced by fibrovascular tissue, and cysts form. The classic radiographic sign is subperiosteal resorption on the radial side of the middle phalanges of the index and middle fingers, with a salt-and-pepper skull and tapering of the distal clavicles. Brown tumors are masses of osteoclast-type giant cells, fibrous stroma, and hemorrhage; hemosiderin from the bleeding gives the brown color. They are reactive, not neoplastic, and regress when PTH falls. Brown tumors can also occur in severe secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism is an appropriate rise in PTH in response to a stimulus outside the parathyroid gland, usually low calcium, high phosphate, or low calcitriol. The glands are behaving normally, so calcium is low or low-normal, never high. The two classic causes are chronic kidney disease (CKD) and vitamin D deficiency, and phosphate separates them.

In CKD, falling glomerular filtration reduces phosphate excretion. Phosphate retention raises FGF23 from osteocytes, and FGF23 together with loss of renal mass reduces 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, so calcitriol falls early. Low calcitriol reduces intestinal calcium absorption and also removes calcitriol's direct suppression of the PTH gene. Phosphate stimulates PTH directly and binds calcium. The parathyroid cells respond with hyperplasia and, over time, express fewer CaSR and vitamin D receptors, so they become harder to suppress.

FGF23 rises; renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase falls
Low calcitriol reduces gut calcium absorption
Low calcium, high phosphate, low calcitriol stimulate PTH
Parathyroid hyperplasia; fewer CaSR and vitamin D receptors
High-turnover bone disease and renal osteodystrophy
blocks.caption: The rise in PTH is appropriate at first; gland hyperplasia is what later allows autonomy.

blocks.text: In vitamin D deficiency (poor sunlight, malabsorption, liver disease), low calcitriol reduces calcium absorption and PTH rises to defend calcium. Because the kidneys work, PTH causes phosphaturia and phosphate absorption from the gut is also low, so phosphate is low. The bone lesion is defective mineralization, osteomalacia in adults and rickets in children.

Renal osteodystrophy is the bone disease of CKD. It includes high-turnover osteitis fibrosa from PTH excess, defective mineralization (osteomalacia), low-turnover adynamic bone disease when PTH is oversuppressed, and mixed forms. Bone also buffers the metabolic acidosis of CKD, adding to mineral loss, and a high calcium-phosphate product promotes vascular and soft tissue calcification.

Tertiary hyperparathyroidism develops when years of stimulation leave hyperplastic, often nodular glands whose set point no longer responds to calcium. PTH becomes very high and calcium rises into the hypercalcemic range. It is seen most often in long-standing dialysis patients and after kidney transplantation, when the new kidney makes calcitriol but the autonomous glands keep secreting PTH.

blocks.title: Reading calcium, phosphate, and PTH
blocks.caption: Calcium tells you whether the gland is autonomous; phosphate tells you whether the kidney is failing.

blocks.predict: A dialysis patient has calcium 8.2 mg/dL (2.05 mmol/L), phosphate 7.0 mg/dL (2.3 mmol/L), and PTH ten times normal. Two years after a successful kidney transplant, calcium is 11.4 mg/dL (2.85 mmol/L) and PTH is still very high. What changed?
blocks.explain: Before transplant this was secondary disease: PTH was high because calcium and calcitriol were low and phosphate high. After transplant those stimuli were corrected, but the hyperplastic glands had become autonomous, so PTH stayed high and now raises calcium. That is tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

blocks.text: Growth hormone (GH) acts in two ways. Its indirect, growth-promoting effects are mediated by IGF-1, made mainly in the liver and also locally in cartilage, which stimulates chondrocyte proliferation, bone growth, and growth of soft tissues and viscera. Its direct effects oppose insulin: GH increases lipolysis and hepatic glucose output and reduces insulin-stimulated glucose uptake. GH excess almost always comes from a somatotroph pituitary adenoma (C08).

Whether GH excess causes gigantism or acromegaly depends only on the epiphyseal growth plates. Before the plates fuse, IGF-1 drives chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate, so long bones lengthen and the child becomes very tall with proportionately large hands and feet; this is gigantism. After fusion, which estrogen completes at the end of puberty, linear growth is impossible. Excess GH and IGF-1 then thicken bone by periosteal (appositional) growth and enlarge cartilage and soft tissue; this is acromegaly. A patient whose disease begins in adolescence and continues into adulthood can show both.

blocks.caption: Visceromegaly and colonic polyps also occur, reflecting IGF-1's growth effects on many tissues.

blocks.text: Cardiovascular disease, chiefly cardiomyopathy, hypertension, and arrhythmia, is the leading cause of death in untreated acromegaly, with respiratory disease and diabetes also contributing. Because the changes are slow, patients often go years before diagnosis, and comparison with old photographs is a classic clue. About a quarter to a third of these tumors also secrete prolactin, and a large tumor can compress the stalk and remove dopamine inhibition, so galactorrhea and hypogonadism may coexist.

A random GH level is unreliable. GH is released in pulses, mainly during slow-wave sleep and after exercise, stress, or fasting, and its plasma half-life is only about 20 minutes, so a single value in a healthy person can be high or nearly undetectable. IGF-1 solves this problem. It circulates bound to IGF-binding protein 3 and an acid-labile subunit, has a half-life of many hours, and therefore integrates GH secretion over the previous day. A raised IGF-1 is the screening test for acromegaly.

IGF-1 must be read against age- and sex-matched ranges. It is physiologically high in puberty and pregnancy, and it is reduced by malnutrition, liver disease, hypothyroidism, poorly controlled diabetes, and oral estrogen, which can mask GH excess.

The oral glucose tolerance test confirms autonomy. In a normal person a 75 g glucose load raises blood glucose, which increases hypothalamic somatostatin and suppresses GH to below about 1 ng/mL (lower cutoffs, about 0.4 ng/mL, apply with sensitive assays). A somatotroph adenoma does not respond to this signal, so GH stays high and sometimes rises paradoxically. After biochemical confirmation, pituitary MRI locates the tumor.

Pituitary MRI, usually a macroadenoma

blocks.caption: Biochemistry first, then imaging, as with Cushing syndrome.

blocks.text: Most somatotroph adenomas are macroadenomas (over 10 mm) at diagnosis. On routine histology they are usually acidophilic (eosinophilic) cells, as normal somatotrophs are. About 40% carry an activating somatic mutation of GNAS, the gene for the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit, which keeps adenylyl cyclase active and mimics constant GHRH stimulation. Rarely, GH excess comes from ectopic GHRH secreted by a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor or bronchial carcinoid, which causes pituitary somatotroph hyperplasia rather than an adenoma.

sections.title: Graves disease versus toxic multinodular goiter

blocks.text: Both Graves disease and toxic multinodular goiter are forms of hyperthyroidism, meaning the gland itself is overproducing hormone. Both show low TSH, from negative feedback of thyroid hormone on thyrotrophs and the hypothalamus, with high free T4 and T3. They differ in what drives the gland and in which tissue responds, and the radioiodine uptake scan shows that difference.

Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism, typically in women aged 20 to 50, and is linked to HLA-DR3 and other susceptibility genes. IgG thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins bind the TSH receptor and activate it as TSH would, through Gs and cAMP. This is stimulatory type II hypersensitivity. Every follicle is stimulated, so the gland enlarges diffusely and becomes highly vascular, often with a bruit, and radioiodine uptake is diffusely increased. Histology shows tall, crowded columnar follicular cells, pale scalloped colloid, and lymphoid infiltrates. T3 production is often disproportionately high.

The extrathyroidal signs are specific to Graves disease because orbital fibroblasts and preadipocytes, and dermal fibroblasts, express the TSH receptor. Autoantibodies and infiltrating T cells activate these fibroblasts to secrete hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans such as hyaluronan, and orbital preadipocytes differentiate into fat. Swollen extraocular muscles and fat push the globe forward, causing proptosis, diplopia, and in severe cases optic nerve compression. The same glycosaminoglycan deposition in the pretibial dermis produces nonpitting pretibial myxedema. Lid retraction and lid lag, by contrast, come from sympathetic overactivity of the smooth muscle of the upper lid and occur in any thyrotoxicosis.

Toxic multinodular goiter arises in a long-standing goiter, usually in an older adult from an area of past iodine deficiency. Some nodules acquire activating somatic mutations of the TSH receptor or Gs alpha and secrete hormone independently of TSH. The resulting suppressed TSH silences the normal tissue, so the scan shows patchy uptake in hot nodules with a suppressed background. An iodine load, as from contrast media, can unmask it. There is no autoimmunity, so there is no ophthalmopathy or dermopathy. A single autonomous nodule is a toxic adenoma.

rows: Autonomous nodules (activating TSH receptor or Gs mutations)
Diffuse, vascular goiter, often with bruit
blocks.caption: Low-uptake thyrotoxicosis (subacute or painless thyroiditis, exogenous hormone) is not hyperthyroidism of the gland and is covered elsewhere (EN-12-C).

blocks.text: Thyrotoxicosis is the clinical state of excess thyroid hormone action from any source. T4 is converted to T3 in tissues, and T3 binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors that pair with the retinoid X receptor on thyroid response elements and change gene transcription. Two groups of target genes explain nearly every finding: those that raise metabolic rate and those that increase sensitivity to catecholamines.

T3 increases synthesis of Na+/K+-ATPase, mitochondrial enzymes, and mitochondria themselves, so ATP turnover, oxygen consumption, and heat production rise. Patients are heat intolerant and sweat, because the body must dissipate the extra heat through cutaneous vasodilation. They lose weight despite a large appetite, since fat and protein are consumed faster than they are replaced, and proximal muscles waste. Gut transit speeds, causing frequent stools.

Circulating catecholamines are normal or low, but tissues respond more strongly. T3 increases beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the heart and alters post-receptor signaling, and it acts directly on cardiac genes, increasing alpha-myosin heavy chain and SERCA2 and reducing phospholamban, which speeds contraction and relaxation. Peripheral vasodilation lowers systemic vascular resistance, so cardiac output rises, pulse pressure widens, and systolic pressure climbs. T3 also shortens the atrial action potential and refractory period, which favors atrial fibrillation, especially in older patients, and can lead to high-output heart failure. Heightened adrenergic responsiveness in the nervous system causes fine tremor, hyperreflexia, anxiety, and lid retraction.

Thyroid hormone increases bone remodeling, activating both osteoclasts and osteoblasts, but resorption exceeds formation, so bone mineral density falls and fracture risk rises, particularly in postmenopausal women. Released calcium can cause mild hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria, which suppress PTH.

blocks.text: Thyroid storm

Thyroid storm is acute, life-threatening decompensation of thyrotoxicosis, usually in untreated or undertreated Graves disease. It is triggered by a stressor such as infection, surgery, trauma, childbirth, an iodine load, or abrupt withdrawal of antithyroid medication, which adds a surge of sympathetic activity and may raise the free hormone fraction. The features are those of thyrotoxicosis pushed past the limits of compensation: high fever, often above 40 °C (104 °F), as heat production exceeds heat loss; tachycardia often above 140 per minute, atrial fibrillation, and heart failure; agitation, delirium, or coma; and vomiting, diarrhea, and jaundice. Hormone levels are not reliably higher than in uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis, so the diagnosis rests on clinical severity. Mortality remains substantial even with intensive care.

ADH (vasopressin) is made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and released from the posterior pituitary when plasma osmolality rises above about 280 to 285 mOsm/kg, or when effective arterial volume falls substantially. It binds V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells, activates Gs and cAMP, and inserts aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane, so water is reabsorbed into the hypertonic medulla. Normally, falling osmolality switches ADH off and a dilute urine excretes the excess water.

In SIADH, ADH is secreted even though plasma osmolality is low and volume is normal. The ADH may come from the tumor itself, as in small cell lung carcinoma, or from the posterior pituitary under abnormal stimulation, as in CNS disease (trauma, stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis), pulmonary disease (pneumonia, tuberculosis), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide, vincristine), and postoperative pain and nausea.

The kidney keeps reabsorbing water, so total body water rises and plasma sodium is diluted. Two-thirds of the retained water enters cells, so the extracellular expansion is modest and there is no edema. That small expansion still raises natriuretic peptides and suppresses renin and aldosterone, and the kidney excretes sodium. This natriuresis brings volume back near normal at the cost of further sodium loss, which is why the patient is clinically euvolemic and why urine sodium is high (usually above about 30 to 40 mEq/L) despite hyponatremia. Serum uric acid and BUN are often low because of the mild volume expansion.

blocks.title: Laboratory criteria for SIADH
rows: ADH acting when it should be off
Water spread across all compartments; escape natriuresis
Hypothyroidism and glucocorticoid deficiency must be excluded
blocks.caption: SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion; glucocorticoid deficiency raises ADH because cortisol normally restrains it.

blocks.title: SIADH among the hyponatremias
rows: Euvolemic, low solute or excess water
blocks.caption: Volume status first, then urine sodium and osmolality.

blocks.text: Symptoms come from the brain. As plasma osmolality falls, water moves into neurons and glia, causing cerebral edema with headache, nausea, confusion, seizures, and coma, most severe when sodium falls quickly or below about 120 mEq/L. Within about 48 hours brain cells export K+ and organic osmolytes to restore volume. This adaptation makes chronic hyponatremia less symptomatic but leaves the brain vulnerable to osmotic demyelination if sodium is raised too fast.

The calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) is a G protein-coupled receptor on parathyroid chief cells and on cells of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. In the parathyroid, rising calcium activates CaSR and suppresses PTH secretion. In the thick ascending limb, CaSR activation reduces the lumen-positive voltage that drives paracellular calcium and magnesium reabsorption, so more calcium is excreted when plasma calcium is high. CaSR therefore sets both the PTH response and the renal response to calcium.

Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) is usually caused by a heterozygous inactivating mutation of CASR, inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. With fewer working receptors, a higher calcium is needed to suppress PTH, so the set point shifts upward. Plasma calcium settles at a mildly raised level with a normal or mildly raised PTH, and magnesium is often high-normal. The kidney also reads calcium as low, so it keeps reabsorbing calcium and urine calcium is inappropriately low.

FHH is usually lifelong, asymptomatic, and benign, with no stones or bone disease, and parathyroidectomy does not correct the calcium because the abnormality is in every chief cell and in the kidney. That is why it must be distinguished from primary hyperparathyroidism before surgery. Infants who inherit two inactivating alleles develop neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism with very high calcium and PTH.

blocks.title: FHH versus primary hyperparathyroidism
rows: Hypercalcemia in relatives, often from childhood
blocks.caption: The urinary calcium measurement is the decisive test.

blocks.title: Calcium to creatinine clearance ratio
blocks.text: A 35-year-old has calcium 10.9 mg/dL and PTH at the upper limit of normal. Her mother has the same finding. A 24-hour urine gives calcium 80 mg/day. The ratio is (urine calcium times serum creatinine) divided by (serum calcium times urine creatinine). With serum creatinine 0.8 mg/dL and urine creatinine 1,200 mg/day: (80 times 0.8) divided by (10.9 times 1,200) equals 64 divided by 13,080, about 0.005. A value below 0.01 means the kidney is retaining calcium despite hypercalcemia, which fits FHH. In primary hyperparathyroidism a high filtered load meets normal CaSR braking of loop reabsorption, so the ratio is usually above 0.02. Ratios of 0.01 to 0.02 are indeterminate.

Puberty begins when the hypothalamic GnRH pulse generator, quiet through childhood, is reactivated. Pulsatile GnRH stimulates gonadotrophs to release LH and FSH, which drive gonadal sex steroid production and gametogenesis. Precocious puberty is traditionally defined as secondary sexual development before age 8 in girls or 9 in boys. Sex steroids accelerate growth and bone maturation, so affected children are tall for age with advanced bone age, but estrogen also closes the growth plates early, which reduces adult height.

Central (gonadotropin-dependent) precocious puberty is the normal axis switched on early. LH and FSH are in the pubertal range, and stimulation with GnRH or a GnRH agonist produces a pubertal, LH-predominant response. Development is consonant, following the normal sequence: breast development first in girls, testicular enlargement (above 4 mL) first in boys because FSH and LH act on the testis. Most cases in girls are idiopathic. Boys more often have a CNS cause, such as a hypothalamic hamartoma, tumor, hydrocephalus, or prior cranial irradiation, so imaging is essential. Loss-of-function mutations in MKRN3, a gene that restrains GnRH, cause some familial cases.

Peripheral (gonadotropin-independent) precocious puberty arises when sex steroids are made without GnRH. These steroids feed back on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so LH and FSH are low and do not rise with GnRH stimulation. In boys the testes stay small because they are not being stimulated, unless the source is in the testis itself. CAH, especially 21-hydroxylase deficiency, causes early virilization from adrenal androgens. McCune-Albright syndrome, from a postzygotic activating GNAS mutation in a mosaic distribution, causes autonomous ovarian estrogen production (most often in girls), cafe-au-lait macules with irregular borders, and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia. Sex steroid secreting tumors of the ovary, testis, or adrenal, hCG-secreting germ cell tumors in boys (hCG acts on the LH receptor), and exogenous hormone exposure complete the list.

Small, unless testicular tumor or hCG source
Idiopathic, hypothalamic hamartoma, CNS tumor, irradiation
CAH, McCune-Albright, gonadal or adrenal tumors, hCG tumors, exogenous steroids
blocks.caption: LH and FSH reveal whether the drive comes from the brain or from the periphery.

blocks.text: Prolonged exposure to sex steroids from a peripheral source can mature the hypothalamus and trigger secondary central puberty, so the two forms can coexist in a child with long-untreated CAH.

integration.text: Every syndrome in this chapter is a failure of negative feedback, and the paired test shows which side failed. Plasma ACTH separates pituitary from adrenal cortisol excess, renin separates adrenal from renal aldosterone excess, PTH read beside calcium and phosphate separates autonomous from appropriate parathyroid activity, TSH with the uptake scan separates gland overactivity from leakage, and LH and FSH separate central from peripheral puberty. Histology supplies the lesions: pituitary, adrenal, and parathyroid adenomas, parathyroid hyperplasia, diffuse thyroid hyperplasia in Graves disease, and ectopic hormone from small cell carcinoma, a neuroendocrine lung tumor. Biochemistry supplies the CAH pathway, genetics supplies CASR, CYP21A2, and GNAS mutations (GNAS links somatotroph adenomas, toxic nodules, and McCune-Albright syndrome through constant cAMP signaling), and immunology supplies the stimulating antibody of Graves disease.

Renal physiology is where most of these diseases become measurable. Aldosterone excess appears as K+ and H+ loss, ADH excess as a concentrated urine with natriuresis, PTH excess as hypercalciuria and phosphaturia, and CaSR loss as hypocalciuria. The limits are equally important. Hormone tests are confounded by circadian rhythm, binding proteins, drugs, illness, and assay differences, so mild abnormalities need confirmation, and imaging follows biochemistry because incidental pituitary and adrenal nodules are common.

summary: Cushing syndrome is confirmed by loss of regulation (high 24-hour urine free cortisol, high late-night salivary cortisol, no suppression with 1 mg dexamethasone) and localized by ACTH: low means adrenal or exogenous, normal or high means pituitary or ectopic.
High-dose dexamethasone suppresses a pituitary corticotroph adenoma but not ectopic ACTH; ectopic ACTH causes hyperpigmentation and severe hypokalemia.
Cortisol excess features follow from protein catabolism, insulin antagonism, fat redistribution, and spillover onto mineralocorticoid receptors.
Primary hyperaldosteronism is hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis with high aldosterone and low renin, without edema because of aldosterone escape; secondary forms have high renin.

In CAH, 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes salt wasting and virilization with high 17-hydroxyprogesterone; 11-beta causes virilization with hypertension; 17-alpha causes hypertension with absent sex steroids.
Primary hyperparathyroidism gives high calcium, low phosphate, and high or inappropriately normal PTH, usually from a single adenoma, with stones, bone disease, and osteitis fibrosa cystica.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism has low or normal calcium with high PTH; phosphate is high in CKD and low in vitamin D deficiency; tertiary disease is autonomous with hypercalcemia.
FHH has mildly high calcium, normal or mildly high PTH, and low urine calcium (clearance ratio below 0.01) from an inactivating CASR mutation, and surgery does not help.
GH excess causes gigantism before epiphyseal closure and acromegaly after; it is confirmed by high IGF-1 and failure of GH to suppress after oral glucose.

Graves disease (diffuse uptake, eye and skin signs) and toxic multinodular goiter (patchy uptake) both give low TSH and high free T4; SIADH gives euvolemic hyponatremia with concentrated urine and high urine sodium; central precocious puberty has raised LH and FSH, peripheral has suppressed LH and FSH.

verify: The 1 mg overnight dexamethasone cutoff (morning cortisol below about 1.8 micrograms/dL, 50 nmol/L) follows Endocrine Society guidance; some texts use 5 micrograms/dL. Confirm the value NABNE expects.

The high-dose dexamethasone test (8 mg, more than 50% cortisol suppression) is largely replaced in practice by CRH stimulation and inferior petrosal sinus sampling; confirm whether NABNE still tests the high-dose test as the discriminator, as the competency states.

Relative frequency of bilateral adrenal hyperplasia versus aldosterone-producing adenoma in primary hyperaldosteronism differs between older and newer sources; this chapter states hyperplasia as the more common cause.

Percentages for primary hyperparathyroidism causes (adenoma about 85%, multigland hyperplasia about 10%, carcinoma about 1%) vary among Robbins (hyperplasia 5 to 10%), Lange, and review books (up to 15%).

The OGTT GH suppression cutoff is below 1 ng/mL in older guidance and about 0.4 ng/mL with sensitive assays; confirm the value NABNE uses. The share of somatotroph adenomas with GNAS mutations (about 40%) and of GH adenomas cosecreting prolactin (about a quarter to a third) varies by series.
SIADH thresholds (urine sodium above 30 versus 40 mEq/L, serum osmolality below 275 mOsm/kg) differ between sources.
FHH calcium to creatinine clearance ratio cutoffs (below 0.01 favoring FHH, above 0.02 favoring primary hyperparathyroidism) are consensus values; other FHH genes (GNA11, AP2S1) are not covered here.
Age cutoffs for precocious puberty (8 years in girls, 9 in boys) are traditional; some pediatric guidance uses lower ages for girls of some populations. Confirm the cutoff NABNE expects.
Thyroid storm fever and heart rate figures are typical values from scoring systems, not diagnostic cutoffs; confirm NABNE expectations if tested.
